title: API Gateway
subtitle: Centralized North-South edge proxy handling auth, rate limiting, TLS termination, and BFF aggregation.
keyTakeaways: An API Gateway shields internal microservices from direct public internet exposure, serving as the single entry point for client traffic.
The gateway centralizes edge cross-cutting concerns: TLS termination, JWT verification, rate limiting, and request correlation IDs.
The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern deploys dedicated gateways per client platform (Mobile vs Web), preventing bloated generic payloads.

sections.heading: Cross-Cutting Edge Responsibilities
sections.body: Exposing dozens of internal microservices directly to the public internet creates major security risks and performance bottlenecks. Clients would have to make multiple network calls over high-latency cellular networks to gather data for a single screen. An API Gateway sits at the perimeter, managing North-South traffic.
bullets: Authentication Offloading: The gateway validates incoming JWTs or OAuth tokens, extracts user claims, and injects trusted internal headers (`X-User-ID`, `X-User-Roles`) before routing to internal services.
Rate Limiting & DDoS Shielding: Enforces token bucket rate limits at the edge, dropping abusive traffic before it consumes internal microservice CPU.
Protocol Translation: Converts external JSON/REST or WebSockets into high-performance internal gRPC messages over HTTP/2.

codeSnippet.title: API Gateway Aggregation Handler (Backend-for-Frontend Pattern)

sections.heading: The BFF Pattern vs Monolithic Gateways
sections.body: Building a single monolithic API Gateway shared by all frontend teams eventually recreates the monolith problem: mobile developers, web developers, and partner integrations fight over configuration files and deployment pipelines.
bullets: Backend-for-Frontend (BFF): Create separate, smaller gateway services tailored to each user experience: Mobile BFF, Web BFF, and Public API Gateway. Each frontend team owns and deploys its own BFF.
Payload Optimization: Mobile BFFs strip unnecessary fields, compress images, and tailor data structures for small screens and spotty cellular networks.
Thin Gateway Rule: Never put business logic or database queries into the gateway. Gateways should perform routing, aggregation, and security only.

tradeOffs.pros: Frontend squads own their gateway; payloads are optimized per device; independent release cycles without deployment blocking.
tradeOffs.cons: Operational overhead of running multiple gateway fleets; potential duplication of authentication code across BFFs.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Enterprises with dedicated mobile and web engineering squads.

tradeOffs.option: Single Centralized API Gateway (Kong / AWS API Gateway)
tradeOffs.pros: Single operational control point; uniform security and rate limiting policies across the company.
tradeOffs.cons: Becomes an organizational bottleneck; payloads compromise between mobile and desktop requirements.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Early-stage startups and smaller engineering teams.

interviewTip: In mobile-heavy system design problems, highlight the BFF pattern: 'To protect mobile clients on high-latency cellular connections from making dozens of API calls, we implement the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern. The Mobile BFF aggregates calls to internal microservices over our private low-latency network and returns a single compact payload tailored for the mobile UI.'
